design-system-accessibility.title: Target conformance level
design-system-accessibility.body:
The WCAG conformance target the team has committed to documented and referenced in contribution guidelines. AA as a baseline for most products, with AAA achievable for specific criteria such as text contrast.

_Tip: WCAG AA is a typical  baseline for most products, with AAA achievable for specific criteria such as text contrast_

design-system-accessibility.title: Colour contrast standards
design-system-accessibility.body:
The contrast ratios verified across all text and interactive element colour combinations (4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text and UI components)

_Tip: Show these ratios in existing UI_

design-system-accessibility.title: Focus indicator design
design-system-accessibility.body:
A visible, high-contrast focus indicator designed for every interactive component

_Tip: Show clear examples for most common interactive components like button and input field_

design-system-accessibility.title: Keyboard navigation patterns
design-system-accessibility.body: Standard keyboard interaction patterns documented and applied consistently e.g. arrow keys for menus and listboxes, Enter and Space for activation, Escape for dismissal

design-system-accessibility.title: ARIA pattern library
design-system-accessibility.body: Attributes that make web content accessible to those who use assistive technologies with roles, states, and properties defined for every interactive component pattern

design-system-accessibility.title: Screen reader testing
design-system-accessibility.body: Components tested with at least VoiceOver on Safari and NVDA on Chrome before shipping

design-system-accessibility.title: Accessibility annotations in design
design-system-accessibility.body: A shared annotation kit used in design files to specify ARIA labels, roles, reading order, and focus behaviour

design-system-accessibility.title: Accessibility in contribution guidelines
design-system-accessibility.body: Ensuring accessibility requirements are part of the component contribution checklist

design-system-accordion.title: Header
design-system-accordion.body:
The clickable area that triggers expanding and collapsing and has a title

_Tip: The header text should clearly convey the content that is inside_

design-system-accordion.title: Expand/collapse icon
design-system-accordion.body: Visual indicator of the current state — typically a plus/minus, or a caret/chevron that rotates between states

design-system-accordion.title: Content area
design-system-accordion.body:
The content that shows or hides when toggled, containing detailed information associated with the header

_Tip: While headers should be text only, content can be anything that is suited to help answer or elaborate on the header (text, image, video, etc)_

design-system-accordion.title: States
design-system-accordion.body: Default (collapsed), expanded, hover, focused, and disabled

design-system-accordion.title: Expanding logic
design-system-accordion.body:
Decide if users can open multiple sections at once, or one at a time

_Tip: Can be determined by whether you think information from other items are related and should be seen together_

design-system-button.title: Base style
design-system-button.body: Your default style, one of the following: fill, outline, underline

design-system-button.title: Shape
design-system-button.body: Visual properties of a button: padding, border, border radius, shadow

design-system-button.title: Variants
design-system-button.body: Each visual type to represent button structure e.g. primary and secondary buttons

design-system-button.title: Copy
design-system-button.body:
Instructional text that details what will happen if you click the button

_Tip: Users should understand what will happen before clicking a button. Buttons can have generic copy such as 'Okay' or 'Cancel', but only if there is context around that action, in the title or as a label for example._

design-system-button.title: States
design-system-button.body: How the button changes based on the interaction: hover, focused, disabled

design-system-color-system.title: Primitive palette
design-system-color-system.body:
A base set of named color ramps (blue-100 through blue-900, neutral-0 through neutral-1000) that serves as the raw material for all semantic decisions

_Tip: Systems where components reference primitive values directly are significantly harder to theme — a color change requires updating each component individually rather than a single token definition_

design-system-color-system.title: Semantic color tokens
design-system-color-system.body:
Named tokens that describe purpose rather than appearance so the system can be reskinned without touching components e.g. color-background-primary, color-text-danger, color-border-interactive

_Tip: The semantic layer is what makes a design system actually themeable by defining purpose for colors_

design-system-color-system.title: Interactive state colors
design-system-color-system.body: Defined color values for default, hover, pressed, focused, disabled, and selected states applied consistently across all interactive elements

design-system-color-system.title: Feedback colors
design-system-color-system.body:
A consistent set of colors for success, warning, error, and informational states — used across alerts, form validation, badges, and status indicators.

_Tip: Feedback colors that pass contrast in light mode frequently fail in dark mode — testing each token pair against every surface in both themes is where most gaps tend to surface._

design-system-color-system.title: Contrast ratios (accessibility)
design-system-color-system.body:
A breakdown of text and interactive element color combinations verified to meet WCAG AA contrast minimums — 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text and UI components

_Tip: Not all colors will pair together nicely so defining this for all usage is helpful_

design-system-color-system.title: Dark and light mode definition
design-system-color-system.body:
A complete parallel set of semantic token values for the opposite mode

_Tip: It is not as simple as inverting colors of one mode to the other, they require their own system (still using the same primitive colors though)_

design-system-color-system.title: Brand color integration
design-system-color-system.body:
Brand colors mapped into the semantic system in a way that maintains accessibility 

_Tip: Where brand values fall below contrast thresholds, they are restricted to decorative contexts, with accessible token values carrying the text and interactive roles._

design-system-color-system.title: Color blindness considerations
design-system-color-system.body:
The palette tested against common color vision deficiencies for when color is used to convey state

_Tip: It's worthwhile considering relative items to the color if vision is a concern, meaning an icon or text can help further convey a state incase the color is not successfully visible_

design-system-input-field.title: Input field
design-system-input-field.body:
Interactive text field for user to enter their data into

_Tip: Ensure text size is readable on all devices_

design-system-input-field.title: Label
design-system-input-field.body:
Stating what information the user is meant to provide

_Tip: Avoid all caps for text labels to improve readability_

design-system-input-field.title: Placeholder text
design-system-input-field.body:
Text inside the input field acting as an example of what you want the user to enter

_Tip: Text colour must be notably lighter than default text, so users don't assume its filled in Providing examples lets users understand how you would like them to enter the information_

design-system-input-field.title: Data format
design-system-input-field.body:
Set text fields to allow the relevant text values e.g. numeric only for phone number

_Tip: Hint at preferred data format with placeholder text or hint_

design-system-input-field.title: Illustration or icon
design-system-input-field.body: A visual cue can help break up a long list of text fields

design-system-input-field.title: Hint
design-system-input-field.body: Elaborate on the title of the text field incase a user struggles to know what to enter

design-system-searchbar.title: Input field
design-system-searchbar.body: A clear container for a user to start typing in

design-system-searchbar.title: Label or placeholder text
design-system-searchbar.body:
Identify the purpose of the field is for them to search

_Tip: Use your placeholder text to suggest examples of what to search for_

design-system-searchbar.title: Quick links, autocomplete and suggestions
design-system-searchbar.body:
As the user is typing, offer available links and phrases based on what they have entered so far

_Tip: With enough data from the user, you can collect quick links and suggestions based on their previous searches to streamline their search_

design-system-searchbar.title: Submit search button
design-system-searchbar.body:
A visible link to submit search and view results

_Tip: Include a loading icon or feature once search has been submitted incase there is a connection issue_

design-system-searchbar.title: Previous searches
design-system-searchbar.body: Showing what a user has searched before can speed up their experience if they frequently search the same queries

design-system-searchbar.title: Appropriate visibility
design-system-searchbar.body: Search should be directly linked to what you are looking for, whether it's searching across the entire platform or in a specific area

design-system-spacing-and-grid.title: Spacing scale
design-system-spacing-and-grid.body:
A defined set of spacing values (typically base-4 or base-8, covering 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 96) used for all margin, padding, and gap decisions

_Tip: A base-8 scale is the most commonly adopted because it divides evenly across common device pixel ratios and helps avoid exceptions being made_

design-system-spacing-and-grid.title: Semantic spacing tokens
design-system-spacing-and-grid.body:
Named tokens for spacing that describe purpose (space-component-padding-sm, space-layout-section-gap) so spacing decisions are intentional, not arbitrary

_Tip: Raw spacing values appearing as hardcoded numbers in components make global spacing changes significantly harder, since each instance requires a separate update rather than a single token edit_

design-system-spacing-and-grid.title: Column grid
design-system-spacing-and-grid.body: A defined column grid for each major breakpoint (typically 4 columns mobile, 8 tablet, 12 desktop) with gutter and margin values specified

design-system-spacing-and-grid.title: Breakpoints
design-system-spacing-and-grid.body:
A named set of breakpoints (sm, md, lg, xl) that are shared between design and code, so responsive behaviour is described in consistent terms across both disciplines

_Tip: Breakpoint names tied to device types (phone, tablet, desktop) tend to age poorly as screen sizes shift. Content-based naming (narrow, mid, wide) describes viewport behaviour rather than hardware categories_

design-system-spacing-and-grid.title: Component vs layout spacing
design-system-spacing-and-grid.body:
A clear distinction between spacing used inside components and spacing used to compose layouts, since different scales often apply to each

_Tip: Buttons that use the same spacing tokens as page-level section gaps, and vice versa, tend to produce compositions where internal padding and layout rhythm feel mismatched_

design-system-spacing-and-grid.title: Density variants
design-system-spacing-and-grid.body: Where applicable, defined compact and comfortable density modes, common in data-heavy products where users need to choose between information density and breathing room

design-system-spacing-and-grid.title: Baseline grid alignment
design-system-spacing-and-grid.body: Text baselines and component heights designed to align to the base unit, so stacking elements produces predictable, harmonious vertical rhythm

design-system-typography.title: Type scale
design-system-typography.body:
A defined set of font sizes with a consistent ratio between them, covering everything from captions to display headings

_Tip: A modular scale (1.25, 1.333, 1.5 ratio) produces a more harmonious hierarchy than arbitrary size choices_

design-system-typography.title: Semantic text styles
design-system-typography.body:
Named styles that describe role rather than size so usage is driven by meaning, not pixel values e.g. display-large, body-default, label-small, caption

_Tip: Style names chosen by size — 24px, 18px, 14px — consistently result in designers selecting styles by measurement rather than role, which makes the system harder to evolve when the scale changes._

design-system-typography.title: Typeface selection and loading
design-system-typography.body: The chosen typefaces detailing style and weight e.g. Inclusive Sans Medium

design-system-typography.title: Line height per style
design-system-typography.body:
Line height defined explicitly for every text style since tightly spaced headings and readable body text require different values

_Tip: Similar style groups follow a consistent line height e.g. 1.5 for body text, 1.2 for heading and 1.1 for display_

design-system-typography.title: Letter spacing per style
design-system-typography.body:
Letter spacing defined per style where needed

_Tip: Similar to line height, where style groups often following a consistent pattern_

design-system-typography.title: Responsive type behaviour
design-system-typography.body: How text styles respond to viewport size, whether through fluid type scaling, breakpoint-based overrides, or fixed sizes with responsive layout compensation

design-system-typography.title: Minimum readable size
design-system-typography.body:
The smallest text size in use across the system, and how readability at that size is validated in the actual rendering environment

_Tip: Consider minimum size between desktop and mobile differently_

design-system-typography.title: Accessibility responsiveness
design-system-typography.body:
How text styles behave at 200% browser zoom, and whether any style communicates meaning through colour variation alone

## Checklist Design · Web app

web-app-settings.title: Structure
web-app-settings.body:
Organising settings controls into logical categories e.g. account, notifications, security, billing.

_Tip: Consider elevating the most commonly changed settings rather than the most important_

web-app-settings.title: Account details
web-app-settings.body: The fields where users update their name, email address, and profile photo

web-app-settings.title: Security details
web-app-settings.body:
The ability to change the password,  two-factor authentication and other security information

_Tip: These fields should require re-authentication to save changes_

web-app-settings.title: Notification preferences
web-app-settings.body:
Controls for which notifications the user receives and through which channel, grouped by type (product updates, reminders, billing)

_Tip: Grouping by type and/or platform helps reduce the chances of a user disabling all notifications rather than some_

web-app-settings.title: Billing
web-app-settings.body: Managing payment method, upgrading or cancelling a payment — this could also be a preview of this information with a link directly to the billing page if separate

web-app-settings.title: Additional preferences (if applicable)
web-app-settings.body: Language, timezone, date format, and appearance settings like dark mode

web-app-settings.title: Danger zone
web-app-settings.body:
Destructive actions like account deletion, clearly separated from the rest of settings

_Tip: Include a confirmation step for any destructive actions, with details on what will be lost if the user continues_

flows-showing-input-error.title: Keep the input in default state
flows-showing-input-error.body: The text field should be checked for errors only after the information has been entered.

flows-showing-input-error.title: Allow user to enter information
flows-showing-input-error.body: Let the user type without interruptions and submit the information aka don't assess as changes are made.

flows-showing-input-error.title: Signal error after loss of focus
flows-showing-input-error.body: After the input has lost focus (user has clicked another element), the field should be assessed. Looks like we have an error here! In this case, explain why the error happened, and what is required to resolve it. For accessibility, combine the text with a visual icon that indicates an error was found.

flows-showing-input-error.title: Return to default state upon reattempt
flows-showing-input-error.body: Once the user focuses on the field again, the error message should disappear. If there is an error again, the process will simply repeat until they are able to continue.

flows-submitting-a-form.title: Show button to submit
flows-submitting-a-form.body: Below the form fields, a button to submit the information needs to be present. You can change the copy to fit the form e.g. the button can say “Subscribe” if someone is providing their email address to receive emails.

flows-submitting-a-form.title: Show loading state after submission
flows-submitting-a-form.body: The user must see the form is in the process of being submitted. Note: also make sure your hover state is considered before they press the button!

flows-submitting-a-form.title: Show success message when it submits
flows-submitting-a-form.body: The form was submitted! Let’s communicate that back to the user with a clear success message.

flows-submitting-a-form.title: If it doesn't, show an error message
flows-submitting-a-form.body: Sometimes, things don’t work out. If the form can’t submit, because of invalid information or another error, that also needs to be shown.

flows-submitting-a-form.title: An error may occur because of the wrong information
flows-submitting-a-form.body: If the criteria for a text field isn’t met, the form can fail to submit due to that error, and must be detailed.
